CHAPTER XLIV. THE WAKING

The fourth night I seemed to fall asleep, and that night woke indeed. I
opened my eyes and knew, although all was dark around me, that I lay in
the house of death, and that every moment since there I fell asleep
I had been dreaming, and now first was awake. “At last!” I said to my
heart, and it leaped for joy. I turned my eyes; Lona stood by my couch,
waiting for me! I had never lost her!--only for a little time lost the
sight of her! Truly I needed not have lamented her so sorely!

It was dark, as I say, but I saw her: SHE was not dark! Her eyes shone
with the radiance of the Mother’s, and the same light issued from her
face--nor from her face only, for her death-dress, filled with the light
of her body now tenfold awake in the power of its resurrection, was
white as snow and glistering. She fell asleep a girl; she awoke a woman,
ripe with the loveliness of the life essential. I folded her in my arms,
and knew that I lived indeed.

“I woke first!” she said, with a wondering smile.

“You did, my love, and woke me!”

“I only looked at you and waited,” she answered.

The candle came floating toward us through the dark, and in a few
moments Adam and Eve and Mara were with us. They greeted us with a quiet
good-morning and a smile: they were used to such wakings!

“I hope you have had a pleasant darkness!” said the Mother.

“Not very,” I answered, “but the waking from it is heavenly.”

“It is but begun,” she rejoined; “you are hardly yet awake!”

“He is at least clothed-upon with Death, which is the radiant garment of
Life,” said Adam.

He embraced Lona his child, put an arm around me, looked a moment or two
inquiringly at the princess, and patted the head of the leopardess.

“I think we shall meet you two again before long,” he said, looking
first at Lona, then at me.

“Have we to die again?” I asked.

“No,” he answered, with a smile like the Mother’s; “you have died into
life, and will die no more; you have only to keep dead. Once dying as we
die here, all the dying is over. Now you have only to live, and that you
must, with all your blessed might. The more you live, the stronger you
become to live.”

“But shall I not grow weary with living so strong?” I said. “What if I
cease to live with all my might?”

“It needs but the will, and the strength is there!” said the Mother.
“Pure life has no weakness to grow weary withal. THE Life keeps
generating ours.--Those who will not die, die many times, die
constantly, keep dying deeper, never have done dying; here all is
upwardness and love and gladness.”

She ceased with a smile and a look that seemed to say, “We are mother
and son; we understand each other! Between us no farewell is possible.”

Mara kissed me on the forehead, and said, gayly,

“I told you, brother, all would be well!--When next you would comfort,
say, ‘What will be well, is even now well.’”

She gave a little sigh, and I thought it meant, “But they will not
believe you!”

“--You know me now!” she ended, with a smile like her mother’s.

“I know you!” I answered: “you are the voice that cried in the
wilderness before ever the Baptist came! you are the shepherd whose
wolves hunt the wandering sheep home ere the shadow rise and the night
grow dark!”

“My work will one day be over,” she said, “and then I shall be glad with
the gladness of the great shepherd who sent me.”

“All the night long the morning is at hand,” said Adam.

“What is that flapping of wings I hear?” I asked.

“The Shadow is hovering,” replied Adam: “there is one here whom he
counts his own! But ours once, never more can she be his!”

I turned to look on the faces of my father and mother, and kiss them ere
we went: their couches were empty save of the Little Ones who had with
love’s boldness appropriated their hospitality! For an instant that
awful dream of desolation overshadowed me, and I turned aside.

“What is it, my heart?” said Lona.

“Their empty places frightened me,” I answered.

“They are up and away long ago,” said Adam. “They kissed you ere they
went, and whispered, ‘Come soon.’”

“And I neither to feel nor hear them!” I murmured.

“How could you--far away in your dreary old house! You thought the
dreadful place had you once more! Now go and find them.--Your parents,
my child,” he added, turning to Lona, “must come and find you!”

The hour of our departure was at hand. Lona went to the couch of the
mother who had slain her, and kissed her tenderly--then laid herself in
her father’s arms.

“That kiss will draw her homeward, my Lona!” said Adam.

“Who were her parents?” asked Lona.

“My father,” answered Adam, “is her father also.”

She turned and laid her hand in mine.

I kneeled and humbly thanked the three for helping me to die. Lona knelt
beside me, and they all breathed upon us.

“Hark! I hear the sun,” said Adam.

I listened: he was coming with the rush as of a thousand times ten
thousand far-off wings, with the roar of a molten and flaming world
millions upon millions of miles away. His approach was a crescendo chord
of a hundred harmonies.

The three looked at each other and smiled, and that smile went floating
heavenward a three-petaled flower, the family’s morning thanksgiving.
From their mouths and their faces it spread over their bodies and shone
through their garments. Ere I could say, “Lo, they change!” Adam and
Eve stood before me the angels of the resurrection, and Mara was the
Magdalene with them at the sepulchre. The countenance of Adam was like
lightning, and Eve held a napkin that flung flakes of splendour about
the place.

A wind began to moan in pulsing gusts.

“You hear his wings now!” said Adam; and I knew he did not mean the
wings of the morning.

“It is the great Shadow stirring to depart,” he went on. “Wretched
creature, he has himself within him, and cannot rest!”

“But is there not in him something deeper yet?” I asked.

“Without a substance,” he answered, “a shadow cannot be--yea, or without
a light behind the substance!”

He listened for a moment, then called out, with a glad smile, “Hark
to the golden cock! Silent and motionless for millions of years has
he stood on the clock of the universe; now at last he is flapping his
wings! now will he begin to crow! and at intervals will men hear him
until the dawn of the day eternal.”

I listened. Far away--as in the heart of an æonian silence, I heard the
clear jubilant outcry of the golden throat. It hurled defiance at
death and the dark; sang infinite hope, and coming calm. It was the
“expectation of the creature” finding at last a voice; the cry of a
chaos that would be a kingdom!

Then I heard a great flapping.

“The black bat is flown!” said Mara.

“Amen, golden cock, bird of God!” cried Adam, and the words rang through
the house of silence, and went up into the airy regions.

At his AMEN--like doves arising on wings of silver from among the
potsherds, up sprang the Little Ones to their knees on their beds,
calling aloud,

“Crow! crow again, golden cock!”--as if they had both seen and heard him
in their dreams.

Then each turned and looked at the sleeping bedfellow, gazed a moment
with loving eyes, kissed the silent companion of the night, and sprang
from the couch. The Little Ones who had lain down beside my father and
mother gazed blank and sad for a moment at their empty places, then slid
slowly to the floor. There they fell each into the other’s arms, as if
then first, each by the other’s eyes, assured they were alive and awake.
Suddenly spying Lona, they came running, radiant with bliss, to embrace
her. Odu, catching sight of the leopardess on the feet of the princess,
bounded to her next, and throwing an arm over the great sleeping head,
fondled and kissed it.

“Wake up, wake up, darling!” he cried; “it is time to wake!”

The leopardess did not move.

“She has slept herself cold!” he said to Mara, with an upcast look of
appealing consternation.

“She is waiting for the princess to wake, my child,” said Mara.

Odu looked at the princess, and saw beside her, still asleep, two of his
companions. He flew at them.

“Wake up! wake up!” he cried, and pushed and pulled, now this one, now
that.

But soon he began to look troubled, and turned to me with misty eyes.

“They will not wake!” he said. “And why are they so cold?”

“They too are waiting for the princess,” I answered.

He stretched across, and laid his hand on her face.

“She is cold too! What is it?” he cried--and looked round in wondering
dismay.

Adam went to him.

“Her wake is not ripe yet,” he said: “she is busy forgetting. When she
has forgotten enough to remember enough, then she will soon be ripe, and
wake.”

“And remember?”

“Yes--but not too much at once though.”

“But the golden cock has crown!” argued the child, and fell again upon
his companions.

“Peter! Peter! Crispy!” he cried. “Wake up, Peter! wake up, Crispy! We
are all awake but you two! The gold cock has crown SO loud! The sun is
awake and coming! Oh, why WON’T you wake?”

But Peter would not wake, neither would Crispy, and Odu wept outright at
last.

“Let them sleep, darling!” said Adam. “You would not like the princess
to wake and find nobody? They are quite happy. So is the leopardess.”

He was comforted, and wiped his eyes as if he had been all his life
used to weeping and wiping, though now first he had tears wherewith to
weep--soon to be wiped altogether away.

We followed Eve to the cottage. There she offered us neither bread nor
wine, but stood radiantly desiring our departure. So, with never a word
of farewell, we went out. The horse and the elephants were at the door,
waiting for us. We were too happy to mount them, and they followed us.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER I. OUTSIDE

‘No room!--Full up!’

He banged the door in my face.

That was the final blow.

To have tramped about all day looking for work; to have begged even for a job which would give me money enough to buy a little food; and to have tramped and to have begged in vain,--that was bad. But, sick at heart, depressed in mind and in body, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, to have been compelled to pocket any little pride I might have left, and solicit, as the penniless, homeless tramp which indeed I was, a night’s lodging in the casual ward,--and to solicit it in vain!--that was worse. Much worse. About as bad as bad could be.

I stared, stupidly, at the door which had just been banged in my face. I could scarcely believe that the thing was possible. I had hardly expected to figure as a tramp; but, supposing it conceivable that I could become a tramp, that I should be refused admission to that abode of all ignominy, the tramp’s ward, was to have attained a depth of misery of which never even in nightmares I had dreamed.

As I stood wondering what I should do, a man slouched towards me out of the shadow of the wall.

‘Won’t ’e let yer in?’

‘He says it’s full.’

‘Says it’s full, does ’e? That’s the lay at Fulham,--they always says it’s full. They wants to keep the number down.’

I looked at the man askance. His head hung forward; his hands were in his trouser pockets; his clothes were rags; his tone was husky.

‘Do you mean that they say it’s full when it isn’t,--that they won’t let me in although there’s room?’

‘That’s it,--bloke’s a-kiddin’ yer.’

‘But, if there’s room, aren’t they bound to let me in?’

‘Course they are,--and, blimey, if I was you I’d make ’em. Blimey I would!’

He broke into a volley of execrations.

‘But what am I to do?’

‘Why, give ’em another rouser--let ’em know as you won’t be kidded!’

The door slammed with the dull, decisive thud of bureaucratic finality.

I stood in the freezing drizzle of the Hammersmith night, calculating the precise rate at which a man’s core temperature drops when he has been walking for fourteen hours on a deficit of three thousand calories. To have scoured the grime-choked streets of London all day for labor was an expected hardship; to have stooped to petition a casual ward for a night on a plank bed was a tactical compromise. To be denied even that miserable sanctuary was merely a lesson in the unreliability of institutional safety nets.

As I mentally mapped the grim reality of my situation, a figure detached itself from the shadows of the brick wall.

“Won’t let you in, eh?”

I turned to assess the man. His shoulders were hunched against the damp, his hands buried deep in the pockets of ruined trousers. He was a veteran of the gutters, worn down to the sinew, reeking of wet wool and cheap gin.

“He claims it’s at capacity,” I replied, my voice steady despite the shivering that had begun to seize my chest.

The man offered a jagged, cynical grin. “That’s the standard deterrent at Fulham. They always say it’s full. Keeps the ledger clean and the workload light.”

I studied him. “You’re suggesting it’s a calculated falsehood? An administrative bluff to filter the weak?”

“I’m saying the bloke’s having a laugh at your expense. If there’s square footage, they’re legally bound to take you. If I were you, I’d ring the bell again and make him do his job.”

There was a certain dark logic to testing the defenses twice. I approached the heavy door and yanked the iron bell-pull. The door swung open almost immediately, revealing the same grizzled pauper who acted as gatekeeper. If he had been the Prime Minister himself, he could not have worn a heavier mantle of unearned authority.

“Here again?” he sneered. “What’s the tactical objective here? Think I’ve got nothing better to do than wait on the likes of you?”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER II. INSIDE

I realised, and, so to speak, mentally photographed all the little details of the house in front of which I was standing with what almost amounted to a gleam of preternatural perception. An instant before, the world swam before my eyes. I saw nothing. Now I saw everything, with a clearness which, as it were, was shocking.

Above all, I saw the open window. I stared at it, conscious, as I did so, of a curious catching of the breath. It was so near to me; so very near. I had but to stretch out my hand to thrust it through the aperture. Once inside, my hand would at least be dry. How it rained out there! My scanty clothing was soaked; I was wet to the skin! I was shivering. And, each second, it seemed to rain still faster. My teeth were chattering. The damp was liquefying the very marrow in my bones.

And, inside that open window, it was, it must be, so warm, so dry!

There was not a soul in sight. Not a human being anywhere near. I listened; there was not a sound. I alone was at the mercy of the sodden night. Of all God’s creatures the only one unsheltered from the fountains of Heaven which He had opened. There was not one to see what I might do; not one to care. I need fear no spy.

The cold was a physical enemy, steadily liquefying the marrow in my bones and draining the last of my cellular energy. But the open window presented a tactical anomaly, and more importantly, a lifeline.

It was a ground-floor sash, thrown wide to the deluge. I had only to breach the perimeter to secure dry cover. There was no watch, no patrol, no sign of life in the immediate vicinity. Out here, I was at the mercy of the elements, another anonymous casualty waiting to be swept into the Thames. The tramp at the casual ward had surrendered his freedom to the constabulary in exchange for a warm cell. I preferred to maintain my operational independence.

Perhaps the villa was empty. Civilian carelessness was a luxury of the secure and the comfortable. I considered knocking to alert the occupants of their vulnerability, perhaps angling for a meager reward. But experience in a harder school had taught me the futility of relying on the gratitude of the comfortable classes. More likely, I would be turned over to the authorities as a vagrant. Better to appropriate the shelter and vanish before dawn.

I leaned over the low brick wall, testing the air. The thermal differential was immediate; warmth bled from the dark aperture. Moving with deliberate silence, I vaulted the barrier. The ground beneath my boots felt cemented and stable. I pressed myself against the exterior masonry, listening at the crevice. Complete silence. It defied logic that any homeowner would leave a ground-floor blind fully raised and the sash open in this weather, but the battlefield is largely dictated by the blunders of the enemy.

A candle drifted through the gloom toward us, carried by unseen currents. Moments later, Adam, Eve, and Mara appeared. They greeted us with a serene good morning, their smiles familiar and comforting; they were accustomed to such transitions.

"I trust you found the darkness pleasant," the Mother observed.

"Not entirely," I admitted. "Yet the emergence from it feels heavenly."

"It is merely the beginning," she corrected gently. "You are hardly awake yet."

"He is already clad in Death," Adam declared, his voice resonant. "Which is the radiant garment of Life." He embraced Lona, placing an arm around my shoulder. He glanced inquiringly at the princess, then patted the head of the leopardess resting nearby. "I suspect we shall encounter you two again shortly," he noted, shifting his gaze between Lona and me.

"Must we die again?" I asked.

"No," he answered, offering a smile identical to the Mother's. "You have died *into* life, and shall die no more. Your task is simply to remain dead—to hold that state. Once we die as we do here, all dying ceases. Now, you must live, and you must do so with every ounce of your blessed strength. The more you live, the stronger you become to continue living."

"But shall I not tire of living so intensely?" I queried. "What if I cease to exert this full effort?"

"It requires only the will; the strength remains inherent!" the Mother insisted. "Pure life possesses no weakness capable of inducing weariness. THE Life continuously generates ours. Those who refuse to die die repeatedly, constantly, sinking deeper into mortality forever; here, everything moves upward, fueled by love and joy."

She paused, her expression softening into a look that conveyed profound intimacy: *We are mother and son; we understand one another. Between us, no farewell is necessary.*

Mara kissed my forehead, her tone buoyant. "I told you, brother, all would be well! When you seek comfort next, say, 'What will be well, is even now well.'" She sighed lightly, and I sensed her unspoken thought: *But they will not believe you!*

"--You know me now!" she concluded, flashing a smile reminiscent of hers.

"I know you!" I responded. "You are the voice crying in the wilderness before the Baptist arrived! You are the shepherd who drives the wandering sheep home before the shadows lengthen and the night deepens!"

"My work shall eventually conclude," she stated. "Then I shall rejoice in the gladness of the Great Shepherd who sent me."

"All night long, the morning approaches," Adam intoned.

"What is that flapping of wings I hear?" I asked.

"The Shadow hovers," Adam replied gravely. "There is one here whom he claims as his own! But once belonging to us, she can never belong to him again."

I turned to gaze upon my father and mother, intending to kiss them before departing. Their couches were empty, occupied only by the Little Ones who had boldly claimed their hospitality. For a heartbeat, the terrible dream of desolation overwhelmed me, and I turned away.

"What troubles you, my heart?" Lona asked.

"Their vacant spaces frighten me," I confessed.

"They departed long ago," Adam explained calmly. "They kissed you before leaving and whispered, 'Return soon.'"

"And I could neither feel nor hear them!" I murmured.

"How could you? You were far away in your dreary old house! You believed the dreadful place had reclaimed you once more. Go now and find them. Your parents, my child," he added, turning to Lona, "must come to find you!"

Our departure hour had arrived. Lona moved to the couch where the Mother who had slain her lay, kissing her tenderly before settling into her father's arms.

"That kiss will summon her homeward, my Lona!" Adam proclaimed.

"Who were her parents?" Lona asked.

"My father," Adam answered, "is also her father."

She turned, placing her hand in mine. I knelt, humbly thanking the three for aiding me in my death. Lona knelt beside me, and together we breathed upon them.

"Hark! I hear the sun," Adam announced.

I listened. He described its arrival as the rushing of ten thousand times ten thousand distant wings, accompanied by the roar of a molten, flaming world millions of miles away. Its approach was a crescendo of a hundred harmonies. The three exchanged glances, smiling, and that smile floated heavenward—a three-petaled flower of familial thanksgiving. From their mouths and faces, it spread across their bodies, shining through their garments. Before I could utter, "Behold, they change!" Adam and Eve stood transformed into the angels of resurrection, while Mara became the Magdalene at the sepulcher.

Adam's countenance flashed like lightning, and Eve held a napkin scattering flakes of splendor throughout the chamber. A wind began to moan in pulsing gusts.

"You hear his wings now!" Adam said, clarifying that he did not refer to the wings of the morning. "It is the great Shadow stirring to depart. Wretched creature, he contains himself and cannot rest!"

"But is there not something deeper within him?" I asked.

"Without substance, a shadow cannot exist—nay, nor without a light behind that substance!" he replied. Listening for a moment, he called out with a joyful smile, "Hark to the golden cock! Silent and motionless for millions of years, he has stood upon the clock of the universe. Now, at last, he spreads his wings! Soon he will begin to crow, and at intervals, men will hear him until the dawn of the Eternal Day arrives."

I listened. Far away—as if within the heart of an aeonian silence—I heard the clear, jubilant outcry of the golden throat. It hurled defiance at death and the dark, singing of infinite hope and coming calm. It was the "expectation of the creature" finally finding a voice; the cry of a chaos destined to become a kingdom! Then came a great flapping.

"The black bat is flown!" Mara exclaimed.

"Amen, golden cock, bird of God!" Adam cried, and the words rang through the house of silence, ascending into the airy regions. At his *Amen*, like doves rising on silver wings from among broken pottery, the Little Ones sprang to their knees on their beds, shouting aloud, "Crow! Crow again, golden cock!" as if they had witnessed and heard him in their dreams. Each then turned to gaze at their sleeping bedfellows, holding them with loving eyes, kissing the silent companions of the night, before springing from their couches.

The Little Ones who had rested beside my father and mother gazed blankly and sadly at their empty spaces for a moment, then slid slowly to the floor. There, they fell into each other's arms, as if seeing and hearing one another anew confirmed their aliveness. Suddenly spotting Lona, they ran toward her, radiant with bliss, to embrace her. Odu, catching sight of the leopardess at the princess's feet, bounded to her side, threw an arm over the great sleeping head, and fondled and kissed it.

"Wake up, wake up, darling!" he cried. "It is time to wake!"

The leopardess remained unmoved. "She has slept herself cold!" he told Mara, casting an appeal-filled look upward.

"She waits for the princess to wake, my child," Mara said soothingly.

Odu looked at the princess and noticed two of his companions still asleep beside her. He flew to them. "Wake up! Wake up!" he shouted, pushing and pulling this one and that. Soon, however, he grew troubled, turning to me with misty eyes. "They will not wake!" he said. "And why are they so cold?"

"They too await the princess," I answered.

He reached across and placed his hand on her face. "She is cold too! What is wrong?" he cried, looking around in dismay.

Adam stepped forward. "Her awakening is not yet ripe," he said. "She is busy forgetting. When she forgets enough to remember enough, she will soon be ready, and wake."
